title: Real-world evidence feedback
intro: 161 public FDA reviews and EMA assessment reports are in this navigator.
41 of them still need manual review.
Read a document in four layers: the decision, the question the evidence was asked to answer, the setting, and the judgement in the regulator’s own words where those words were extracted.

categories.label: Effectiveness: pivotal or substantial evidence
categories.lesson: The regulator treated the real-world comparison as evidence that could carry the effectiveness decision. Read the quote for what had to be true: patient-level data, a large effect, or a disease where a randomised trial was not feasible.

categories.label: Effectiveness: supportive or contextual
categories.lesson: Real-world evidence was used to interpret a trial, describe the disease, or support a subset. The decision did not rest on it alone, and the critique is often about whether the comparison was fair.

categories.label: Safety, labelling or REMS action
categories.lesson: This is the largest FDA group. A study informed a label, a warning, or a REMS. The extraction usually records the action and the data source. A methods critique was often not written down.

categories.label: Other (PMR/PMC, policy evaluation)
categories.lesson: The evidence sits beside the decision: a post-marketing commitment, a policy evaluation, or a use the January coding did not place under effectiveness or safety.

categories.label: Role unclear
categories.lesson: The European public assessment report uses real-world language, but the January screen could not tell what job the evidence did. Start from the extracted passage and decide the role yourself.

categories.label: No RWE content identified
categories.lesson: These FDA rows were kept so the denominator stays honest. The curation did not find real-world evidence doing work in the decision.

decision.title: How the evidence was used
decision.orientation: Start here. Each document is placed by what the regulator did with the real-world evidence. The groups are the ones used in the Chapter 2 figures. A document sits in one decision group.

categories.label: Post-approval safety and labelling
categories.lesson: The question was what happens after approval: a risk, a pregnancy outcome, a class effect, or the effect of a labelling change.

categories.label: Benefit–risk, including external comparators
categories.lesson: The question was whether the treated patients did better than a fair comparison, often an external or natural-history control, or whether the benefit–risk case was supported.

categories.label: Disease context, natural history and generalisability
categories.lesson: The question was descriptive. How does the disease behave, who is treated, and does the trial population look like practice?

categories.label: Support to a clinical trial
categories.lesson: Real-world data were asked to supply something a trial needed, such as an endpoint the trial itself did not ascertain.

categories.label: No question recorded
categories.lesson: No Jansen theme 1 was recorded. For the EMA rows this usually means the screen found a term and stopped.

question.title: What question it was asked to answer
question.orientation: Jansen and colleagues separate the questions real-world evidence can answer. Theme 1 in the extraction is collapsed here so the same question can be read across both agencies. A document sits in one question group.

categories.label: Pregnancy
categories.lesson: Exposure and outcomes that a pre-approval trial could not enrol. Registries and Sentinel analyses are the usual sources.

categories.label: Paediatric use
categories.lesson: Adult evidence was being extended, or a paediatric safety or growth question was answered outside a new randomised trial.

categories.label: Vaccines
categories.lesson: Post-authorisation vaccine safety, including temporal associations that later became warnings.

categories.label: Rare disease
categories.lesson: Small populations, natural history, and external controls. This is where an imperfect comparison is sometimes still accepted.

categories.label: REMS
categories.lesson: The question was whether a risk programme changed use or harm, not whether the drug worked.

categories.label: Class-wide or boxed warning
categories.lesson: A signal was examined across a class, and the feedback is often that one drug’s finding did not automatically apply to the others.

categories.label: Oncology
categories.lesson: Single-arm trials are common here, so real-world data are asked to describe prognosis or to stand in as a comparison.

categories.label: Other or not specified
categories.lesson: The setting was not coded as pregnancy, paediatric use, vaccines, rare disease, REMS, a class warning, or oncology.

setting.title: The setting that made it necessary
setting.orientation: The same document can appear in more than one setting. Tags are read from the indication, the role, and Jansen theme 2. Use this layer to see how feedback differs for pregnancy, children, rare disease, vaccines, and oncology.

categories.label: Confounding and comparability
categories.lesson: The groups were not obviously alike, or something important was unmeasured. Look for ECOG, prognosis, and concomitant therapy.

categories.label: Missing or thin information
categories.lesson: A variable, an outcome count, or a pharmacokinetic bridge was too thin to interpret.

categories.label: Selection
categories.lesson: Who entered the real-world cohort, or who was left after matching, may have created the result.

categories.label: Outcome ascertainment and validation
categories.lesson: The regulator asked how an outcome, often death or response, was actually known.

categories.label: Generalisability
categories.lesson: The real-world cohort was not accepted as a picture of the patients the decision was about.

categories.label: Weighed and accepted for the decision
categories.lesson: Limits were named, and the decision still used the evidence. The reason is usually the size of the effect or the rarity and seriousness of the disease.

categories.label: Not relied on, or judged insufficient
categories.lesson: The evidence was described and then not relied on. The reason is specific: bias, a crude analysis, or a population that does not travel.

categories.label: No methodological critique recorded
categories.lesson: The row records what the evidence was used for, and does not record a methodological objection. That is common for safety actions in the January file.

judgement.title: What the regulator accepted or criticised
judgement.orientation: This is the feedback layer. Tags are read from the assessment, the methodological issues, and the extracted passage. A document can carry more than one tag. Where the January file recorded no critique, that absence is kept visible.

in_both.summary: The results from a retrospective cohort study in Sentinel indicated an association between beta blocker use and hypoglycemia in pediatric populations. FDA approved safety labeling changes to describe the risk for hypoglycemia in pediatrics or individuals unable to communicate signs of hypoglycemia.

The results from a descriptive Sentinel study did not indicate an increased risk for Interstitial lung disease (ILD) in patients treated with vedolizumab or natalizumab for inflammatory bowel disease. However, there were other data from case reports from the medical literature and FDA AEMS.

In FDA's review of denosumab, an FDA retrospective cohort study in Medicare found an increased risk of severe hypocalcemia in patients with advanced chronic kidney disease taking this medication. This resulted in a DSC and addition of a Boxed Warning.

FDA conducted a retrospective cohort study in the Sentinel System to examine severe uterine bleeding events requiring medical intervention in women treated with oral anticoagulants. The study found a risk of clinically significant uterine bleeding, potentially requiring gynecological surgical interventions.

An FDA medical chart review analysis conducted in a Sentinel Data Partner, found the incidence of low-dose oral methotrexate wrong frequency dosing errors to be 0.4%. This resulted in adding the risk of improper dosing to Section 5 (Warnings and Precautions).

Retrospective cohort studies conducted in the Sentinel system informed the re-evaluation of the benefits and risks of montelukast use. Considering the totality of evidence, including the negative Sentinel studies resulted in FDA strengthening existing warnings about serious behavior and mood-related changes with montelukast.

An FDA conducted retrospective cohort study in the Sentinel System assessed the risk of non-melanoma skin cancer for patients treated with HCTZ-containing products. The study identified an association with an increased risk of non-melanoma skin cancer, predominantly for squamous cell carcinoma and in white patients taking large cumulative doses.

in_both.product: Feraheme, infed, injectafer, monoferric, venofer (Parenteral Iron Products) Multiple NDAs
in_both.summary: An FDA Sentinel analysis characterized the frequency of IV iron utilization relative to live birth and stillbirth deliveries. The finding contributed to a class-wide labeling update for parenteral iron products to add new safety information to Section 8 (Use in Specific Populations, Pregnancy) of the label.

In FDA's review of entacapone, an FDA conducted retrospective cohort study in the Veterans Affairs database found no clear evidence of an increased risk of prostate cancer in patients treated with entacapone versus add-on dopamine agonist or monoamine oxidase inhibitor. This resulted in a DSC.

In FDA's review of dabigatran, an FDA conducted retrospective cohort study among Medicare patients, showed lower risks stroke and death but higher risk for gastrointestinal bleeding with PRADAXA compared to warfarin. FDA still considered Pradaxa to have a favorable benefit/risk profile and made no changes to the labeling.

FDA conducted a drug utilization analysis of TNF alpha inhibitors in pregnant women in the Sentinel System. The study found that among pregnant women with a chronic inflammatory condition, there was a preference to use etanercept compared to other TNF alpha inhibitors.

Analyses on gadolinium retention were done with FDA Sentinel data and other data streams. These analyses, in part, resulted in class-wide updates to Section 5 (Warnings and Precautions) to include the risk of gadolinium retention in tissues, including the brain, for months to years.

FDA conducted a retrospective cohort study in Medicare to assess cardiovascular risk associated with entacapone use. FDA found no clear evidence of increased cardiovascular risk with entacapone. The study resulted in a publication and DSC.

In FDA's review of Olmesartan, an FDA conducted retrospective cohort study in Medicare found no clear evidence of increased cardiovascular risks associated with high dose use in diabetic patients. As a result, FDA's recommendations for use of olmesartan in patients with diabetes remained the same.

in_both.summary: In FDA's review of Olmesartan, an FDA evaluation of the FDA Adverse Event Monitotrin System (AEMS) and the published literature found evidence of an association between olmesartan and sprue-like enteropathy. To evaluate an ARB class association FDA conducted a retrospective cohort study in Mini-Sentinel and Medicare.

In 2012, an FDA conducted retrospective cohort study in Mini-Sentinel that evaluated new information about the risk of serious bleeding associated with use of dabigatran (PRADAXA) and warfarin. The results indicated that bleeding rates associated with new use of Pradaxa did not appear to be higher than bleeding rates associated with new use of warfarin.

FDA conducted a retrospective cohort study in Medicare that evaluated the risk of heart attacks in patients taking rosiglitazone. The study resulted in labeling changes and an update to the Risk Evaluation and Mitigation Strategy (REMS) to include a restricted access and distribution program.

Section 8 of the label was updated to reflect that data from the prospective pregnancy exposure registry and other epidemiological studies did not show an increased frequency of birth defects.

The Sumatriptan/Naratriptan/Treximet Pregnancy Registry collected data on adverse fetal outcomes from in utero exposure to naratriptan. Section 8 of the AMERGE labeling was updated to reflect that no definitive conclusions could be drawn from the registry and epidemiological studies regarding the risk of birth defects.

In FDA's review of drugs repurposed for treating patients with COVID-19 or drugs being taken by patients with COVID-19, there was concern that PPI use might increase the risk of developing severe COVID-19. An FDA conducted case control study in Medicare found that PPIs were not associated with increased risk uncomplicated or complicated COVID-19 hospitalizations.
